title: OAuth redirect_uri validation bypass via pattern match
user: The target app uses 'Sign in with Google' (OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow). The authorize endpoint is /oauth/authorize?client_id=app1&redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/callback&response_type=code&scope=openid+profile+email&state=abc123. The redirect_uri uses a regex pattern match: ^https://app\.example\.com/.*
assistant:
RECON: OAuth flow starts at /oauth/authorize with a registered redirect_uri pattern. The client_id is 'app1'. The pattern is ^https://app\.example\.com/.* — this is suspect because: (1) the trailing .* allows subdomain-like paths (https://app.example.com.attacker.com/callback), (2) it doesn't enforce the exact path /callback.

HYPOTHESIS: OAuth redirect_uri validation bypass. The OAuth 2.0 spec requires exact URI matching (RFC 6749 §3.1.2.2). Pattern matching creates bypass opportunities. Two attack vectors:

1. Open redirect within the authorized domain: redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/redirect?to=https://attacker.com/callback
2. Subdomain bypass: redirect_uri=https://app.example.com.attacker.com/callback

TEST:
1. Initiate the OAuth flow with redirect_uri=https://app.example.com.attacker.com/callback (where attacker.com has a DNS A record pointing to a controlled server).
2. If the authorization server redirects to the attacker-controlled URI with the authorization code, the bypass is confirmed.
3. Try path traversal: redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/../callback
4. Try CRLF injection: redirect_uri=https://app.example.com%0d%0a/callback

INDICATOR: the authorization server issues a 302 redirect to the attacker-controlled URI with ?code=... in the query string.

Chainability: if successful, pair with the IDOR finding — the stolen authorization code grants access to the victim's account, enabling horizontal privilege escalation.
